title: Concurrency bisection and microburst playbook
content:
SUMMARY:
This note captures an experimental, operational procedure we can follow when trying to find the practical concurrency breakpoint for a model+hardware combination and to validate our microburst resilience. It intentionally trades exhaustive statistical rigor for speed and repeatability in the lab. The goal: a short, repeatable recipe that engineers and SREs can run in ~2–4 hours to identify the maximum sustained concurrency, burst handling characteristics, and dominant bottleneck signals to investigate further.

WHY THIS IS DIFFERENT:
- Most existing docs focus on long, plateau-style runs. This playbook uses a bisection approach to converge quickly on the break point and pairs it with targeted microburst injections to stress transient queuing and scheduling logic.
- Emphasizes observable signals and quick heuristics (GPU IPC, host runnable, NVLink saturation, batch queue depth) rather than trying to measure single-number TPS in noisy environments.

ASSUMPTIONS & SCOPE:
- Target workload: autoregressive transformer (8k context) with typical production caching disabled for the baseline.
- Environment: Dedicated GPU node (A100x1 or H100x1), latest inference runtime build, and standard system telemetry (nvidia-smi, dcgm, perf counters, host dstat).
- This is a lab procedure — run against a fresh environment snapshot where possible (no competing pods, pinned CPU governors).

HIGH-LEVEL PROCEDURE:
1) Sanity checks (10–15m)
   - Confirm pinned model version and runtime commit. Record hashes.
   - Clear any KV caches and disable global response caching.
   - Ensure node has stable thermals and no noisy neighbor processes.
   - Launch basic smoke run at concurrency=1 for 3 minutes and capture baseline latency distribution.

2) Establish starting range (15–30m)
   - Run short stepped runs to bracket the breakpoint: try concurrencies [1, 4, 8, 16, 32] for 2 minutes each.
   - Observe where p95 latency jumps >2x or GPU utilization crosses ~85% while queue depth increases. Use these observations to pick low and high bounds for bisection.

3) Bisection sweep to converge on steady breakpoint (45–90m)
   - Use bisection rather than linear climb: pick midpoint of current bounds, run for N=6 minutes (2 min warmup + 4 min sample).
   - Measurement window: ignore first 2 minutes to allow priming (see warmup section). Collect per-request latency, token throughput, GPU utilization, IPC, SM active cycles, and host runnable threads.
   - If p95 < target_slo (for test baseline) and GPU util < 92% and queue depth stable, set lower bound = midpoint; else set upper bound = midpoint.
   - Repeat until bounds converge within ±10% or for max 6 iterations.

4) Microburst injection (30–45m)
   - At the converged concurrency, inject controlled microbursts: short (5–15s) 3x and 6x transient spikes while monitoring queue depth and request tail latency.
   - Two patterns: single-node spike; multi-client staggered spike (simulate many clients that backoff).
   - Criteria: if p99 during microburst exceeds steady p99 by >3x or request queue depth grows without drain for >30s, classify as "microburst vulnerable". Capture timeline traces.

5) Saturation long run (optional, 60–120m)
   - Run sustained at 90% of converged concurrency for 1 hour to observe drift, OOM patterns, memory leaks, and control-plane interactions.

INSTRUMENTATION (minimum signals to capture)
- Host: top/psutil snapshot every 5s, dstat for per-cpu load and io, netstat for socket backlogs.
- GPU: DCGM metrics (utilization, sm_efficiency, mem_used, dram_throughput), nvidia-smi sampling every 1s.
- Runtime: token emit timestamps, request enqueue/dequeue timestamps, batch sizes, queue depth, worker idle/active durations.
- Tracing: sampled end-to-end spans with tags: concurrency_level, client_id, batch_id, entered_queue_at, started_on_device_at, finished_at.

WARMUP GUIDELINES (practical)
- Cold-start priming: before any measured run, do a scripted warmup that runs 20 synthetic requests with a mixture of short and long sequences to bring GPU kernels and cuBLAS caches to a quasi-steady cache state.
- Measured runs should include a discard period of the first 2 minutes (empirically chosen) to avoid priming skew. For very short microbenchmarks (<4m total), increase priming to 5 minutes.
- RNG/seed hygiene: keep a fixed seed set for generation prompts across runs to make sequence length and branching consistent; record the seed in run metadata.

DECISIONS & HEURISTICS
- Use median of p95 across samples rather than single-run p95 to reduce single-run noise.
- Prefer GPU-bound identification: if SM efficiency < 60% but GPU util >80%, suspect kernel-level stalls (memory stalls, serialization).
- If host load >70% and runtime threads are runnable, suspect CPU scheduling or Python GIL hotspots.

COMMON TROUBLE SIGNALS & FIRST INVESTIGATIONS
- Rising queue depth + stable GPU util: investigate batch aggregation logic and per-worker dequeue rate.
- Short bursts of 100% GPU util followed by idle: look at serialization points (locks, GC pauses, model init).
- Persistent high host run queue: check CPU affinity and isolate runtime to dedicated cores.
- NVLink/interconnect saturation: check dram throughput and PCIe counters; consider pinning model shards differently.

REPRODUCIBILITY CHECKLIST
- Record: git commit, model checksum, runtime config, node image, CUDA/cuDNN versions, BIOS power profile, and ambient temp if available.
- Capture deterministic client config: seed, arrival pattern, payload sizes.
- Save a copy of the exact load generator config and invocation command.

SAMPLE COMMAND SNIPPETS (lab use only)
- Start DCGM recorder: dcgmi dmon -e 1000 -f dcgm-1s.csv
- Run loadgen: ./bench-client --model-checksum ab12cd --concurrency 24 --duration 360 --arrival poisson --seed 42 --out events.csv
- Tail runtime logs: kubectl logs -f deployment/inference-runtime --since=10m | grep "enqueue" > runtime-enqueue.log

DOCUMENTATION ARTIFACTS TO PRODUCE AFTER RUN
- Short run summary (1 page): breakpoint concurrency, p50/p95/p99, GPU signals, verdict (ok/needs-optimizations/microburst-vulnerable).
- Full artifact bundle: dcgm CSVs, events.csv, runtime traces (OTLP export), and a short notes.txt with next steps.

OPEN QUESTIONS / ACTION ITEMS
- Action: Add automated quick-bisection to bench-harness to reduce manual decision-making (Rohit).
- Question: Should priming use realistic cache-warm sequences (user traffic style) or synthetic seeds? Experiment needed (Linnea).
- Action: Add NVLink/PCIe telemetry into the default bench artifact bundle (Marco).

QUICK TROUBLESHOOT FLOW (if breakpoint unexpectedly low)
1) Run smoke at concurrency=1; if baseline p95 is high, fix model/runtime before prodding.
2) Check host CPU steal/IO wait.
3) Check for background cron jobs / backup processes.
4) Repeat bisection using smaller step durations to isolate transient scheduling.

NOTES TO SELF (informal)
- Keep runs short in noisy lab machines; if the node is shared, results vary widely.
- We should push a minimal bench-harness PR that emits the required tracing fields; eliminates many post-hoc correlation steps.

REFERENCES
- Internal: bench-harness design docs (see linked PR), occupancy calibration notes in confluence.
- External: microburst literature on networked systems — useful analogies for our burst handling problem.

END.
